title: Threat actors: who they are, what they want
body_md:
## Who is behind it matters less than what they’d get

Ask people to picture an attacker and most will draw a hooded figure over a keyboard. The email in your inbox comes with no portrait. It comes with grammar, a logo and a request, and from those you can’t tell a bored teenager from a crime syndicate from a state. You don’t have to.

A *threat actor* is whoever carries out or directs a harmful action. Some want money and go after it with mass messages or long, patient conversations. Others want access, data, influence, disruption or revenge. An insider can abuse access they legitimately hold, and a colleague’s hijacked account can deliver an attacker’s request without the colleague knowing. Treat these as hypotheses, not labels you can pin on someone from a single email. Flawless grammar is no evidence of a state, and clumsy wording doesn’t make a request harmless.

Opportunistic mass fraud, organized criminal operations, state-backed activity and malicious insiders are all useful categories when evidence supports them. Their motives and capabilities overlap: a state link doesn’t require a zero-day, and an insider may use perfectly ordinary, approved tools.

So instead of sorting senders into types, start with **asset, capability, opportunity and consequence**. What could the requester gain: a password, a payment, a document, access to a device, a change to an approval process? What access would let them do it? Where could you cut the chain? A student with one account and a finance clerk who approves invoices face very different consequences from emails that look alike. Match the safeguard to the action: unique passwords and multi-factor sign-in (MFA) for account access, normal approvals and a callback for payment changes, minimal access for shared documents.

### A motive doesn’t identify a message

Money drives fake jobs, invoice diversion and extortion. Someone else may be after publicity, ideological disruption or information. In real investigations motives are often mixed, or never found out. Don’t decide a request is safe because the supposed sender has no reason to hurt you. And don’t assume a well-known person must be the target of a sophisticated actor. Public and private accounts alike deserve basic controls, while people who face targeted risk may need advice from their own organization.

The FBI describes business email compromise as a pattern in which an apparently trusted business message is used to redirect money. A real mailbox may have been taken over, so checking only the sender’s address is weak. An internal request can just as easily be genuine. What matters is whether a high-impact change went through the established process and was confirmed through contact details you already trust.

### The limits of attribution

An IP address, a writing style or a time zone can mislead. Proxies, shared tools and copied text break the simple inferences. Incident teams can weigh evidence over time; as an ordinary recipient you usually need to decide only whether to grant access or authorize a change. Don’t post accusations based on a single message. Keep the relevant records privately, and bring in the service or organization if you suspect a real incident. Naming the culprit can wait for people who hold the evidence. The file, the account and the payee are yours to protect now.

widget_config.goal: Pick the protection from the asset and the action being requested, not from a guess about who is attacking or why.
widget_config.today_action: Write down two accounts or work processes you control that would hurt to lose, and one independent way to confirm a high-impact change.
widget_config.scope: General teaching on how to think about threats. The people in the cases are invented. Actor labels are provisional, and the US FTC and FBI examples are bound by American reporting and legal rules.

sources.title: NCSC: How to spot a scam email, text message or call
sources.scope: UK consumer guidance, published in 2021 and reviewed in 2022. The habit of verifying independently applies well beyond the UK.

sources.title: UK NCSC: Fundamentals of cyber risk
sources.scope: UK guidance on organizational risk. Capability, intent, motivation and opportunity are treated as parts of the analysis.

sources.title: FBI IC3: Business Email Compromise
sources.scope: A US law-enforcement overview. Verifying a payment change works the same way anywhere.

sources.title: FTC: What is a money mule scam?
sources.scope: A US consumer warning from 2020. Banking and legal consequences depend on where you live.

blocks.title: A colleague’s profile asks for the client list
blocks.situation: A message in the work chat, sent from a colleague’s profile, asks Sam to export the client list to a shared folder he doesn’t recognize before a meeting.
blocks.analysis: It could be a hijacked account, an impersonator, or the colleague making an honest mistake, and nothing in the message says which. The asset is client data. Sam should use the approved sharing process and confirm the request in the company directory before exporting anything.

blocks.title: A temporary analyst with a ticket
blocks.situation: A temporary analyst on a documented project asks for read-only access to one report. The project owner confirms it in the usual ticket, and the access can expire when the work ends.
blocks.analysis: This can be entirely legitimate. Narrow, time-limited access, granted after normal approval, handles the risk without guessing at anyone’s motive or stalling the project.

blocks.title: Capability first, motive later
blocks.setup: An invented school club keeps event payments and member contacts. A new request arrives, apparently from a volunteer.

steps.prompt: The volunteer asks for the full member contact file “for coordination.” What do you work out first?

choices.text: Decide from the request alone that the volunteer is a criminal.
choices.consequence: You have accused someone without a scrap of evidence.
choices.explanation: A broad request may be a mistake or may be malicious; either way it needs checking.

choices.text: Pin down what data is requested, for what purpose, and what the club’s access rules say.
choices.consequence: You know what would leave the group, and why.
choices.explanation: The asset and the access matter more than a guess about the sender’s motive.

steps.prompt: The request arrives from the volunteer’s usual account. What now?

choices.text: Confirm the task through the club coordinator’s established channel.
choices.consequence: You test both the need and the state of the account.
choices.explanation: A genuine account can be misused, or the request can simply be a mistake.

choices.text: Send the file, since the username matches.
choices.consequence: The file is gone before anyone has checked purpose or authority.
choices.explanation: A familiar account isn’t enough to justify exporting sensitive data.

steps.prompt: The coordinator says all the volunteer needs is a head count. If you sent the full file in the last step, that is a separate problem. What now?

choices.text: Send the whole contact list in a personal chat anyway.
choices.consequence: The full file is exposed, or exposed a second time if it already went out.
choices.explanation: Counting people doesn’t take their personal contact details.

choices.text: Give just the number in the approved workspace, and tell the coordinator about any earlier file you sent.
choices.consequence: This task runs on the minimum of data, and any earlier leak is flagged so it can be contained.
choices.explanation: An earlier mistake doesn’t justify handing over more, and it deserves a real response.

steps.prompt: Later the volunteer asks to change the account that receives ticket money. What check applies?

choices.text: Use the club’s payment-change approval and a callback to a number you already have.
choices.consequence: The money change gets its own scrutiny.
choices.explanation: Someone can be authorized for one task and not for another.

choices.text: Accept it; the request comes from a familiar account.
choices.consequence: A familiar username ends up standing in for authority over a separate financial change.
choices.explanation: Even a legitimate earlier request wouldn’t authorize a new payee.

blocks.debrief: Replay it and watch the target shift from contact data to money. A familiar sender doesn’t make every request equal; each asset gets its own control.

questions.prompt: A message has polished language and a custom logo. What does that tell you about the actor?

choices.text: Very little. Decide from the access being requested and an independent check.
choices.explanation: Polish doesn’t establish skill, identity or motive.

choices.text: It must be a state actor.

questions.prompt: A known vendor’s mailbox sends new payment details. What is the main risk?

choices.text: Only a forged sender address; if it matches, the check is over.
Payment diversion, even if the mailbox is genuine. Verify through a contact you already have.
choices.explanation: A hijacked real account can carry fraudulent details.

questions.prompt: A temporary contractor asks for the one report named in an approved ticket. What is the best response?

choices.text: Grant just the approved scope and expiry through the normal controls.
choices.explanation: Legitimate work can go ahead with bounded access.

choices.text: Refuse all contractors, since insiders are a threat category.
choices.explanation: A category is not evidence against this particular request.

questions.prompt: What can you conclude from one suspicious IP address or time zone?

choices.explanation: A network location doesn’t name an individual.

choices.text: It’s a lead for investigators, not a reliable way to name the actor.
choices.explanation: Shared infrastructure and proxies muddy attribution.
